name: SolarWinds
blurb: Draft exercise based on the documented incident “SolarWinds” (CTID Attack Flow corpus). A well-known supply chain attack against an Austin, TX software company.

injects.title: Malware
injects.text: Attackers embedded their malicious payload on a legitimate component of the SolarWinds Orion Platform software. This component is a DLL library,… To bypass application control technologies, adversaries sign their malware with valid signatures by creating, acquiring, or stealing code-signing… The malicious DLL file was distributed to victims through an automated update mechanism.

injects.title: Time Based Evasion (Time Based Checks)
injects.text: Once loaded, the backdoor runs a series of checks to ensure it is running in an actual environment. The backdoor also checks that the last write-time. The backdoor checks for a variety of antivirus/endpoint detection agents prior to execution (e.g. Windbg, Autoruns, Wireshark). The backdoor conducts basic reconnaissance on the compromised system to determine running processes to report to the C2 server.

injects.title: Domain Generation Algorithms
injects.text: Adversaries use DGAs to dynamically generate a C2 domain rather than relying on static IP addresses. The C2 responds with an encoded buffer of commands for the backdoor to execute. The commands allow the attackers to run, stop, enumerate processes;… The attackers used a legitimate hostname found within the victim's environment as the hostname on their C2 infrastructure to avoid detection. injects.text: The attackers used valid accounts to move laterally. When executed during lateral movement, rundll32 ran through WMIC. The Cobalt Strike beacon was loaded onto the machine. According to Microsoft, the Cobalt Strike DLL was likely deleted after execution to avoid forensic discovery.
